extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate and graduate students in mathematical logic / computability
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook exposition covering extensions of first-order logic (second-order, higher-order, intuitionistic, modal), their semantics and derivation-systems, plus an introduction to recursive (computable) functions (primitive recursion, composition, unbounded search). Provides definitions, examples, and key theorems about expressiveness and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order language: quantification over relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of second-order logic allows quantification not just over a domain of individuals, but over relations on that domain as well: for each k one adds variables R which range over k-ary relations, and allows quantification over those variables; if R is a variable for a k-ary relation and t1,...,tk are first-order terms, Rt1...tk is an atomic wff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality is only a primitive symbol for first-order terms; equality between relation variables R and S of same arity k is an abbreviation for ∀x1...∀xk (Rx1...xk ↔ Sx1...xk). The quantifier rules extend to the new second-order variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension schema (second-order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehension schema: for each wff α (in which R is not free) include an axiom of the form ∃R ∀x1...∀xk (α(x1,...,xk) ↔ R x1...xk). Equivalently, allow the inference α[λx.β(x)/R] ⊢ ∃R α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehension permits formation of relations defined by formulas; in full generality it is impredicative (α may quantify over relations including R), which prompted predicative restrictions historically. If R is allowed to occur in α the comprehension schema is inconsistent (exercise noted). Comprehension axioms must be present in the second-order part of structures for the system to be sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of second-order derivation systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Two natural choices for derivation systems: (1) a 'minimal' second-order derivation system together with some comprehension axioms; (2) the 'standard' second-order derivation system with full comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors often assume item (2) when unspecified. One can study weaker subsystems by including only particular comprehension axioms; completeness/soundness behavior depends on these choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order semantics: weak vs standard (full)
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic choices: (1) weak semantics — a structure is a first-order structure plus a second-order part big enough to satisfy the chosen comprehension axioms; (2) standard (full) semantics — the second-order part consists of all relations on the first-order domain (full structures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard/full semantics yields categorical descriptions of many mathematical structures but the standard derivation system is not complete for it (no effective complete system). The minimal derivation system is complete for the weak semantics (viewing second-order as many-sorted helps show this). If comprehension axioms are included in the derivation system, semantics must be restricted to structures satisfying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order axioms for arithmetic (categoricity under full semantics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms for arithmetic that, together with the second-order induction axiom ∀R ((R0 ∧ ∀x (Rx → Rx')) → ∀x Rx), provide a categorical description of the standard model B of arithmetic under full second-order semantics: list of arithmetic axioms (1) ∀x ¬x' = 0, (2) ∀x ∀y (s(x) = s(y) → x = y), (3) ∀x (x + 0) = x, (4) ∀x ∀y (x + y' ) = (x + y)', (5) ∀x (x × 0) = 0, (6) ∀x ∀y (x × y' ) = ((x × y) + x), (7) ∀x ∀y (x < y ↔ ∃z y = (x + z')).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under full semantics these axioms + induction determine the standard model up to isomorphism (proof sketch via defining injection f : N → |A| and using fullness to get the inductive set P in the second-order domain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressiveness vs meta-theoretic drawbacks of second-order logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-order logic is much more expressive than first-order logic: can quantify over sets/functions, express induction, finiteness, well-ordering, connectedness, and give categorical descriptions (e.g., reals as complete ordered field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawbacks: no effective derivation system complete for full second-order semantics; many first-order meta-properties fail (compactness, Löwenheim–Skolem). Weak semantics offers completeness for minimal derivation systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order logic as many-sorted logic (translation device)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-order logic can be viewed as a many-sorted logic: one sort for 'objects' and for each k a sort for 'k-ary relations'; include built-in relation symbols true_k R x1...xk to assert R holds of x1,...,xk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With this identification, the weak second-order semantics corresponds to the usual many-sorted semantics and can be embedded in first-order logic, which helps establish completeness of the minimal system for the weak semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-order logic: finite types formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite types are defined inductively: (1) N is a finite type; (2) if σ and τ are finite types then so is σ → τ; (3) if σ and τ are finite types then so is σ × τ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: N denotes natural numbers, σ → τ denotes functions from σ to τ, σ × τ denotes ordered pairs. Types serve as syntactic labels classifying domain objects and allow higher-type expressions (functions of functions, functionals, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-type term formation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms are built inductively with rules: (1) variables of each type; (2) 0 is term of type N; (3) S (successor) of type N → N; (4) Rst as term of type N → σ when s is σ and t is N → (σ → σ) (primitive recursion operator); (5) application s(t) when s: τ→σ and t: τ; (6) λx.s is term of type τ→σ when s:σ and x:τ; (7) ⟨s,t⟩ is term of type σ×τ; (8) projections p1,p2 for pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rst denotes the function defined by primitive recursion (Rst(0)=s, Rst(x+1)=t(x,Rst(x))). λ-abstraction provides comprehension-like definitions of functions. Wffs are then equalities s=t between terms of same type plus connectives and higher-type quantifiers. Axioms govern the basic equations for these term constructors and standard quantifier/equality rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-order semantics: full vs weaker
rubrics_metrics.description: Full higher-type semantics: variables of type σ→τ range over all functions from objects of type σ to objects of type τ. Weaker semantics: a structure gives sets T_τ for each type τ and appropriate operations for application/projection, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with second-order logic, full semantics is too strong for any effective, complete derivation system; weaker semantics can be arranged to admit completeness theorems for suitable derivation systems. Higher-type logic naturally embeds much mathematics and has useful constructive/intuitionistic interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: BHK (constructive) interpretation for intuitionistic connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive (Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov) interpretation: a proof of α ∧ β is a proof of α paired with a proof of β; a proof of α ∨ β is either a proof of α or a proof of β together with explicit information which; a proof of α → β is a procedure transforming proofs of α into proofs of β; a proof of ∀x α(x) is a procedure returning a proof of α(x) for any x; a proof of ∃x α(x) is a value x together with a proof that α(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates intuitionistic restrictions: e.g., existence proofs must provide a witness; disjunction requires choosing a disjunct. The Curry–Howard isomorphism/wffs-as-types paradigm formalizes these computational interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-negation translation (classical → intuitionistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive translation α ↦ α^N: atomic α ↦ ¬¬α; (α ∧ β)^N ↦ (α^N ∧ β^N); (α ∨ β)^N ↦ ¬¬(α^N ∨ β^N); (α → β)^N ↦ (α^N → β^N); (∀x α)^N ↦ ∀x α^N; (∃x α)^N ↦ ¬¬∃x α^N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key theorems: (1) α ↔ α^N is classically provable; (2) if α is classically provable then α^N is intuitionistically provable. Extension: if Γ proves α classically then Γ^N proves α^N intuitionistically (Theorems 124C and 124D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kripke semantics for intuitionistic logic (structure and forcing clauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Kripke structure M = ⟨W, R, V⟩ consists of a set W, a partial order R on W with a least element, and a monotone assignment V of propositional variables to nodes. Forcing M,w ⊩ α is defined inductively: (1) M,w ⊩ p_i iff p_i is assigned to w; (2) M,w ⊮ ⊥; (3) M,w ⊩ (α ∧ β) iff M,w ⊩ α and M,w ⊩ β; (4) M,w ⊩ (α ∨ β) iff M,w ⊩ α or M,w ⊩ β; (5) M,w ⊩ (α → β) iff for all w' ≥ w, if M,w' ⊩ α then M,w' ⊩ β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: worlds/states of knowledge ordered by extension; monotonicity ensures known truths persist to future states. Use Kripke models to show non-validity (e.g., provide counterexample to ¬(p∧q) → (¬p ∨ ¬q)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal logic: operators, Kripke semantics, and axiom/frame correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: Modal propositional logic adds □ (necessity) operator: if α is wff then □α is. ♢α abbreviates ¬□¬α. Kripke semantics for modal logic uses a set of possible worlds P and an accessibility relation Rxy; □α is true at a world if α holds in all accessible worlds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of systems and frame conditions: S4 adds axioms □(α→β)→(□α→□β), □α→α, □α→□□α and the rule 'from α conclude □α' — corresponds to reflexive, transitive frames; S5 further adds ♢α→□♢α and corresponds to universal accessibility. Different axiom choices suit different interpretations (provability, epistemic, temporal, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive recursion: pattern and uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive recursion defines functions h(x0,...,x_{k-1},y) by two equations: h(...,0)=f(x0,...,x_{k-1}) and h(...,y+1)=g(x0,...,x_{k-1},y,h(...,y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the immediately preceding value h(...,y) may be used in the second equation. The natural numbers' induction principle guarantees uniqueness and totality of the function defined. Examples: add and mult are given by primitive recursion (add(x,0)=x; add(x,y+1)=succ(add(x,y)); mult(x,0)=0; mult(x,y+1)=add(mult(x,y),x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of number-theoretic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is k-place and g0,...,g_{k-1} are n-place functions, define h(x0,...,x_{n-1}) = f(g0(x0,...,x_{n-1}),...,g_{k-1}(x0,...,x_{n-1})).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If f and all gi are computable (or primitive recursive), then h is too: compute each yi = gi(...) then apply f to (y0,...,y_{k-1}). Composition is a closure operation used in building primitive/general recursive functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbounded search and recursive functions (partial and general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding unbounded search (μ-operator / unbounded minimization) to primitive recursion yields partial recursive functions; restricting to those partial recursive functions that happen to be total gives general recursive (total recursive) functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recursive (partial/total) functions capture the intuitive notion of computability: they can simulate other models of computation (Turing machines, lambda calculus, etc.), and general recursive functions are exactly the total ones among partial recursive functions.
